title: Asymmetric quantum cloning on orthogonal orbits and four-mode fermionic states
abstract: In this work, we study asymmetric $(1\to2)$ quantum cloning for pure states belonging to orbits generated by the orthogonal group. For every dimension $(d\geq3)$, we determine the full region of achievable pairs of average single-copy fidelities. Using orthogonal covariance and the Brauer algebra, we reduce the optimization over all CPTP maps to a finite-dimensional spectral problem and construct explicit optimal cloning channels. We then apply the general results to four-mode fermionic states in the even-parity sector. Using triality, we identify the fixed-concurrence fermionic families with the orthogonal orbits considered in the first part of the paper. In particular, for pure Gaussian states we show that the symmetric locally optimal cloner is unique. We also compare local and global cloning and find that the channel optimal for the joint two-copy fidelity is different from the one optimal for the single-copy fidelities. Finally, we show that the locally optimal cloner cannot be implemented using only operations which preserve fermionic Gaussian states.
summary: This paper rigorously determines the achievable fidelity region for asymmetric quantum cloning when the input states are constrained to specific orbits of the orthogonal group. By employing advanced algebraic techniques involving the Brauer algebra, the authors derive explicit optimal cloning channels. The results are then applied to the physical system of four-mode fermionic states, establishing fundamental limits on quantum state duplication for these systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the achievable fidelity region for asymmetric quantum cloning processes ($1 	o 2$) applied to pure states residing on orbits generated by the orthogonal group $O(d)$. It specifically applies these general results to four-mode fermionic states.
main_result: The full region of achievable average single-copy fidelities is determined by solving a spectral problem derived from the Brauer algebra. The optimal cloner for the joint two-copy fidelity is shown to be different from the one optimal for single-copy fidelities.
method: The authors reduce the optimization over all CPTP maps to a finite-dimensional spectral problem using orthogonal covariance and the Brauer algebra. They characterize the achievable region using a support function derived from the Uhlmann–Jozsa fidelity.
model_or_system: The primary model is the quantum cloning process ($\Phi: ho_\psi 	o ho_{AB}(\psi)$) acting on states $\psi$ belonging to orbits $O(d)_q$ generated by the orthogonal group $O(d)$. The specific application involves four-mode fermionic states in the even-parity sector.
key_observables: Average single-copy fidelities ($F^A, F^B$), the two-copy moment ($\mathcal{M}^{(d)}_2(q)$), and the support function $h_{O(d)}^q(a, b)$.
important_parameters: The dimension $d \ge 3$, the orbit parameter $q(\psi) = |\psi^T \psi|^2 \in [0, 1]$, and the fidelity parameters $a$ and $b$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the input state $\psi$ is drawn from the invariant measure $\mu_q$ on the orbit $O(d)_q$, and the optimization is performed over CPTP maps.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the operational setup for asymmetric one-to-two cloning. Figure 2 illustrates pairing diagrams in the Brauer algebra $B_3(d)$ related to the cloning process.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework for asymmetric cloning on $O(d)$ orbits, determining the fidelity region via spectral methods. It then applies these general results to the specific case of four-mode fermionic states, utilizing triality to connect the two analyses.
why_interesting: This work provides deep connections between quantum information theory (cloning bounds) and representation theory (Brauer algebra, orthogonal groups), which is highly relevant for understanding fundamental limits in quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Operational setup for asymmetric one-to-two cloning on an orthogonal orbit. The channel maps the unknown input ρψ to a joint state on A⊗B, which is not assumed to factorize. The downward branches denote partial traces: discarding A gives clone B, while discarding B gives clone A. The pointwise overlaps are fA(ψ; Φ) and fB(ψ; Φ); their orbit averages are the fidelities in Eqs. (10) and (11).

FIG. 2. Pairing diagrams in B3(d). Each diagram has three upper (output) and three lower (input) vertices, ordered from left to right. Upper row: the identity, transposition s12, and contraction e12; each leaves the third tensor factor unchanged. Lower row: multiplication by vertical concatenation. The hollow circles mark the identified vertices. Summing the common index around the closed loop contributes d, giving e2 12 = de12.

FIG. 4. Optimal symmetric local fidelity for the four-mode family, with q = C2 +. The circle, square, and triangle mark the Gaussian orbit q = 0, the projective 2-design orbit q = 2/9, and the maximal-concurrence orbit q = 1, respectively. The dashed vertical line locates the unique minimum at q = 2/9, where the second moment equals the Haar moment.

FIG. 3. Pareto boundaries in the (FA, FB) plane for three d = 8 orthogonal orbits, corresponding through triality to three four-mode fermionic concurrence classes. The solid curve is the Gaussian orbit q = 0; the dashed curve is the projective 2-design orbit q = 2/9, with the universal eight-dimensional average local-fidelity boundary. The dash-dotted curve is q = 1, the real-state ensemble in orthogonal coordinates. The inset uses the same axes and resolves the Gaussian and 2- design curves near equal fidelities.

FIG. 5. Average local fidelity versus average global fidelity on the four-mode Gaussian orbit, restricted to the covariant channels Φc with real coefficients c = (x, x, z)T and cT G8c = 1. These channels are output-exchange symmetric and have Choi rank eight. The solid and dashed curves are the + and − branches of Eq. (107). The diamond at their common right endpoint marks the global optimum; the circle marks the unique local optimum. The inset separates these points. The plotted curves describe only this family of channels and not the full set of attainable local–global fidelity pairs.
